name: Netherlands
title: The Netherlands: high non-EU fees, and the scholarships that cover them
lede: Dutch universities teach hundreds of programmes in English, but students from outside the EU/EEA pay institutional fees that are often €12,000–€30,000 a year. The funded routes are university scholarships such as TU Delft's Van Effen and Maastricht's NL-High Potential.
description: Tuition fees for non-EU students in the Netherlands and the full scholarships at TU Delft and Maastricht University that cover tuition and living costs.
card: Non-EU master's fees often €12,000–€30,000; full awards at TU Delft and Maastricht cover them.

sections.html: EU/EEA students pay the Dutch statutory fee (€2,694 for 2026–27). Students from outside the EU/EEA pay an institutional fee set by each university, for master's programmes usually somewhere between about €12,000 and €30,000 a year, depending on the university and subject.

Two routes on this board cover tuition and living costs:

  • TU Delft's Justus & Louise van Effen Excellence Scholarship: about 16 awards across two-year MSc programmes; apply with a complete MSc application by 1 December.
  • Maastricht University's NL-High Potential Scholarship: 18 awards for 2027–28 covering tuition, living expenses (€15,925 for a 13-month programme), insurance and visa costs; master's application by 10 December, scholarship by 1 February.

Dutch scholarship deadlines fall months before regular admission deadlines, and you normally need a complete admission application first. For a September start, have your transcripts, English test and references ready by November of the previous year.
Student housing is scarce in Delft, Amsterdam, Utrecht and other university cities. Look as soon as you are admitted, and be wary of listings that ask for payment before you have seen a contract.

sections.h: Proof of funds for your residence permit
sections.html: The Dutch immigration service (IND) asks you to show the study norm: €1,130.77 a month for university and higher professional education in 2026, the most a Dutch student can receive in study finance when living away from home. You need it for a year (twelve times the monthly amount, €13,569.24), and in practice you usually transfer it to your university, which applies for the permit for you. The amount changes every 1 January.

You may work as an employee only if your employer has a work permit (TWV) for you, and then you must choose: up to 16 hours a week, or full time in June, July and August. Self-employment does not need a work permit, as long as you still meet the conditions of your study permit.

sections.h: After you graduate: the orientation year
sections.html: Within three years of finishing your studies, you can apply for a residence permit for an orientation year for highly educated persons. It lasts one year, and during it you may work freely: your employer does not need a work permit.

faq.q: How much money do I need for a Dutch student residence permit?
faq.a: The 2026 study norm for university and higher professional education is €1,130.77 a month, and you need it for a year: €13,569.24.

faq.q: Can I work while studying in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Only if your employer gets a work permit for you, and then up to 16 hours a week or full time in June, July and August.

faq.q: Can I stay in the Netherlands after graduating?
faq.a: Yes. Within three years of graduating you can apply for a one-year orientation year, during which you may work without a work permit.
